utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Registrar, could you call the case, please. And good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Oric, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour, distinguished gentlemen. I am able to follow the proceedings completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and good morning my learned friends of the Defence team. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers and Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, I thank you, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning to my colleagues from the Prosecution. I am Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones I represent the Defence team of Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our Case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you. Can we bring in the witness straight away or are there any further matters? I see no --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No preliminaries today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any preliminaries from Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning, everybody. I would like to ask a question, with your indulgence, right at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Radic -- good morning to you, Mr. Radic, and welcome back here. What would you like to ask? How can I help you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think you are able to help me. I made a mistake yesterday, and I apologise for it. I would appreciate very much an opportunity to correct it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. Radic. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question was asked concerning the person named Mrki. There were two persons, Mrki and the chief. So I was thinking of one person and I sort of replayed the whole thing last night, and I must say I remember Mrki was in a combat uniform whereas the chief was in civilian clothes. And I would like to make this correction in my testimony. I hope you will forgive me for my error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Radic. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But before you proceed, let me have this clear in my mind. But you also here told us yesterday, again if I remember well, but usually my memory doesn't fail me much, but you also told us yesterday that there was no way you were speaking of two Mrkis, only one Mrki.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I said. In fact, I said unless there are two persons named Mrki. And that's when it comes to the mistake I make -- I made distinguishing between Mrki and the chief. The chief was in civilian clothing and Mrki was in uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was the name of the chief? Do you know it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure. I think his name was Mirzat or Mirsad, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Radic. Ms. Sellers, I apologise to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just ask, and I think that Your Honour already has done that, what the witness has just come back to clarify be incorporated in the record within the context of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Sellers: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, yesterday the Chamber listened to audiotapes of a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. conversation about prisoner changes. Now I would like to ask you some questions about that audiotape. At one point in the tape a voice says, and I would say that both Defence counsel and the Chamber have copies, written copies of the transcript, but I'm referring to page 5 of that transcript. The ERN number on the transcript is 0168415, 0164 -- I'm sorry. This will help: 01168415 to 01168421. Now, at one point a voice on that transcript, Mr. Radic, says: "I'm Veselin Sarac from Podravanje. There is also Nedjelko Radic from Cikota. There is also a man from Indjija, who came here to work, to help." Did you recognise the voice that said that phrase on the audiotape?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Trial Chamber who was speaking at that point.

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veselin Sarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the same Veselin Sarac who was imprisoned with you while you were at the SUP in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the same Veselin Sarac who later spoke to you, after he had been released, that he had participated in conversations relating to a possible exchange? Is that the same Veselin Sarac?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, also on the tape that we listened to yesterday there was someone who identified themselves as Cakura.

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise the person's voice who identified himself as Cakura?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because I had known Cakura for quite a while, so I recognised him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the same Cakura who you earlier testified as being from Zeli [phoen] who had captured a bus from the bauxite mine and was active in the SDA?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, do you know a man named Rad Bjelanovic? No, Bjelanovic. Excuse my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this man, Mr. Bjelanovic, did he work at the bauxite mine?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did, and I know him because we had lived in the same town for 30 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it that you've had conversations with him or you have otherwise listened to his voice?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. He was my manager in the bauxite company for three years. We saw each other every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise his voice on the audiotape that we listened to yesterday?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the person who identified himself as Bjelanovic?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Rade or Radomir Bjelanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever come to find out that Rade or Radomir Bjelanovic had been involved in negotiating prisoner exchanges in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out after the exchange when we arrived in Milici at the SUP. He was the manager then, the chief, and he told me that we had negotiated our exchange with Cakura and Mr. Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise the other voice that was on the tape that identified itself as Naser?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in your conversations, after your release, to Mr. Bjelanovic, did he give you the impression that he was certain that he had spoken to Cakura and to Naser Oric about this prison exchange?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Bjelanovic said that he had talked with them, with Cakura and with Naser, but I cannot confirm that because I didn't know Naser and I cannot identify his voice one way or another. It's Bjelanovic, B-j-e-l-a-n-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radic. Now, Mr. Radic, the person on the tape who identifies himself as Naser says that "there's a detainee from Zenica who most probably will be released today at the exchange." And at this point I'm referring to page 8 of our transcript, almost at the bottom of the page, transcript of the audiotape. Now, Mr. Radic, you testified previously that there was a prisoner from Zenica in the room to the right of yourself. To your knowledge, was that prisoner released from detention before you and the other men in your cell were released from detention?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many days after you arrived in the prison that the man or the detainee from Zenica was released? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say exactly. It was a long time that I spent there, but I think he was released after four or five days. I'm not quite sure, but soon after I arrived -- in fact, he was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, you also testified that Mr. Sarac, Nevenko, Zoran Bankovic, yourself, were continuously beaten in the prison starting on the evening of September 25th. By the time the prisoner from Zenica was released, would it be your testimony that you had received several beatings before his release?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to recall the other part of the conversation that Mr. Veselin Sarac transmits over the radio. It's on page 5 of the transcript. He says: "Nobody has harmed us. We are well for now and you can talk with me some more or the Comrade Naser." Wasn't it true by this time when Veselin Sarac says that, he had already been beaten several times in the prison?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That statement made by Veselin Sarac is not correct. We were beaten several times up to that day when he went to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also on page 5 of the transcript, there is a voice that has N in front of it, we presume that of Naser Oric as one of the four voices on the tape, that says: "So one of your people is here. He is, he has come here, so this is just to convince you that they are alive and well and that nobody has touched them." Mr. Radic, would it be your opinion that this statement that "nobody has touched them" would be untrue at the point in time that this audiotape was made?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Up to that time when Sarac went for negotiations, Kukic had already been killed and of course we had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to the next area of his testimony at this point in time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please do, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you testified previously that you saw the person referred to as Naser Oric three times during your stay at the SUP building. Now, could you please describe for the Trial Chamber the third occasion on which you saw Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third time was on the 15th in the evening, because we were exchanged on the 16th. I don't remember what time it was. At night all five of us were taken out or called out of our cells, and we were taken to that room with the wood-burning stove where we found Mr. Naser Oric, Kemo, I believe Mrki was there, too, but I'm not sure. And they lined us up. And then Mr. Naser asked each one of us in turn whether we knew this man, I believe his name was Akif Hrustic. Of course I didn't know him. I had never been to Srebrenica before that. Three other prisoners didn't know him either. There was a man from Indjija, there was a postman from Fakovici, and I believe Sarac was the only one who knew him. I later found out that Sarac indeed knew both Akif and his father. Thereupon Mr. Naser Oric said to Sarac: You must know him. His father is a butcher. But Sarac said: No, I don't. And then Naser struck him only once with the back of his hand. And then he grabbed him by the foot for a moment, lifted it, held it like that for a second, and then let go. That was the third time that Mr. Naser came to visit in that entire period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did Mr. Naser Oric strike Veselin on his face or on his chest or on another part of his body?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice because I wasn't really paying attention -- in fact, I didn't dare to look. I think he struck him on the face. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after Mr. Sarac was struck, did he remain standing or did he fall down or did he sit down?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He remained standing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after Naser Oric struck Mr. Sarac, what did you and the other detainees do or say?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't say anything. We kept quiet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how long were you in the room with the wood-burning stove along with Naser Oric, Kemo and Mrki on this third occasion?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's just that my learned friend keeps referring to Naser Oric. It should be clear that this is the person who called himself Naser. There was never any identification by this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I agree with that, Your Honour, I'm sorry. Referred to as Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Point taken. The Trial Chamber notes it. In any case, Ms. Sellers, throughout almost, with a few exceptions here and there, you know, as always, the man who described himself as Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted that to remain clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask, how long were you in the room, you and the other prisoners, with the man who referred to himself as Naser Oric, with Kemo, and Mrki on this third occasion?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't stay there for a long time after that incident with Sarac. They returned us to our cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone else, any of the other prisoners who were with you, were they physically mistreated on that occasion in the room with the person who referred to himself as Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you referred to the date of the 15th. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, would that be the 15th of what month and what year, please?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 15th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you referred to the date of your exchange as the 16th. Would you please confirm for the Trial Chamber that would be the 16th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The very next day, the 16th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, were you and Zoran Brankovic, the postman, Nevenko, and Veselin Sarac released from the prison on the following day?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber how you left the prison.

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next morning Cude arrived, the keyturn of the prison. He unlocked our cell and told us that we would be exchanged. At first I couldn't believe this. We all came out into the hall. He had a bottle of water. He poured some water for us to wash. Outside the main entrance to the SUP building there was a lorry parked; it was yellow, the FAP type. We brought it, the lorry -- actually we hoisted Nevenko's body up because he couldn't climb himself, and then the four of us boarded the lorry. We stayed there for about ten minutes and then Kemo arrived and he told Zoran Bankovic and Mr. Sarac to get off the lorry. They got off, he took them back to the same room inside the SUP building. They stayed for a couple of minutes. And then Kemo ordered me and the postman to get off, too, to hoist Zoran Bankovic's body up onto the lorry and Veselin Sarac, too. Nevenko was unable because he had been beaten badly. So we lifted them onto the lorry one by one. This probably meant that they had been beaten on the day of our exchange. Once we got them onto the lorry, Kemo sat down inside the cab with the driver, and we took off to our exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you taken to to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We arrived in a place called Potocari. They parked the lorry outside a house. Kemo was off somewhere, carrying the megaphone. I'm not sure where he was off to. When he returned about 20 minutes later, he told us that he had gone to negotiate with the Serbian side and something to the effect that they would not have us back. He was probably just trying to frighten us. We waited there for another hour or thereabouts, and then we set out on that same lorry, and Kemo, naturally, was with us. We reached a place called Zuti Most, which is in the vicinity of Potocari. We arrived. We got off the lorry, the two of us, and we carried the three other men down from the lorry and sat them down on the ground. At that moment, a car appeared, a Serbian police car. As far as I know, a police officer named Jokic from Bratunac was there. Behind the car, there was a tractor carrying 20 dead bodies. Among those dead bodies, there was also the body of Akif Hrustic. I apologise. I believe the last name is Hrustic. This is something I found out later. I found out that he was uncle of Mr. Naser Oric. At least, that's what I heard. I have no idea whether it's true or not, but that's what I heard. We were then exchanged for those dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you eventually taken to Bratunac that day of your exchange?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in Bratunac, were you still with Nevenko, Veselin Sarac, with Zoran Bankovic, and with the person you referred to as the postman?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were all at the hotel in Bratunac. We were put up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the prisoners who came to Bratunac with you taken to a hospital or a medical facility to treat any of their injuries?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That same evening Slavenko was taken to Zvornik, to the hospital there. He died several days later. The same evening the postman was visited by some relatives of his and he left with them. Veselin Sarac, Zoran, and myself remained at the hotel until the next morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the hotel, did anyone interview you about what had happened at the prison in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a man there I didn't know. I later found out that he was a journalist. He put a mike in front of me, a microphone or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether this journalist also interviewed Veselin Sarac or Mr. Nevenko or the other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present when these interviews were taking place?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were all in the same room. The first questions were addressed to Sarac, because he was the one who looked the most badly beaten of all of us. I assume Nevenko came up next, and then he asked me questions, too. I don't think he asked Zoran any questions, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, before you, Mr. Sarac, or Nevenko were asked questions, did the people in the Bratunac hotel physically mistreat you or try and alter your appearance or in any way try and frighten you or make you have the appearance of someone who was frightened?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you were interviewed along with Mr. Sarac or Mr. Nevenko, did anyone at the hotel tell you what to say or how to answer any questions?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't even know that a journalist would be there to interview us. We were put into a room and perhaps half an hour later the journalist came along. There was a boy who worked at reception and there were two of my relatives who had heard of the exchange, of the exchange to take place, and they came over to be there. But no one mistreated us or beat us there. How could they have done anything like that? We were, after all, on Serbian territory. We were on the Serbian side now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now like to show the exhibit Prosecution -- one minute, Your Honours. This will be Prosecution Exhibit 98, and I do have a revised transcript of that exhibit I would like to pass on. May we proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, Ms. Sellers. Yes, Ms. Sellers, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I'm going to ask you to look at the images that are going to appear on the screen in front of you and to please listen to the audio part of these images.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Can we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we have a slight problem. There is no audio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We certainly don't have audio, but it isn't running. We're just having a still there, a still shot of --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We'll proceed for one more second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, we can hear it, but it is low --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It's very low. Might I ask Mr. Radic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to hear that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can barely hear it myself and I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can barely hear it myself, so we need to increase the volume -- is it possible to increase the volume? We can make adjustments -- one moment. No, I don't think we can make adjustments on what we have here because it's only the colour management. Yeah, I think it should work now. Try it, please. But, Ms. Sellers, we can hear more or less some of the words but we don't have the video now. No, I tried.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We have the video and the muffled words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's try it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I would like to ask you, are you able to hear the video?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of it, but I understand some bits and pieces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I would ask you to pay as close attention as possible. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber if you recognise the person whose image you see in front of you now.

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veselin Sarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the person you've identified as Veselin Sarac's face, would it be your testimony that he received what looks -- appears to be bruises on his face from beatings administered at the prison in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, because no one beat us at the hotel in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Please continue the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can we just go forward for two more Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. seconds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, if you were able to listen to that last part of the conversation, where in the transcript it refers to a person supposedly Naser Oric who hit Mr. Sarac, is it your opinion that they're referring to that incident that happened on the third time that you were in the presence of the person referred to as Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't think this witness should offer his opinion as to what's being discussed. He's given his evidence about what he saw and I don't see how this line of questioning will be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can rephrase it a little bit different, whether it reflects actually what he saw. I can't tell you myself how to rephrase it, obviously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, this last part of the conversation where it speaks of a person supposedly Mr. Naser Oric having hit Mr. Veselin related to someone named Akif Hrustic, does that reflect what occurred or what you testified occurred on the third time that you were with the person supposedly called Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the story rings true. He says that it was on the same evening and he refers to Akif, which means that it must have been the same evening that Mr. Naser struck him. I think I did say a while ago in my testimony I believe he struck him on the face once. And in connection with Akif, he says on this tape that he did know him but he couldn't remember at the time. It's true that it was on the evening of the 15th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We can continue now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I would ask you now to look at the screen and could you please tell the Trial Chamber, if you know, who is this person in the image before you?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Nevenko, the man from Indjija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is the Nevenko who was imprisoned with you in the Srebrenica SUP?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I would like to ask you, do you recognise the person who's in the image before you now?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. That's me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you wearing what appears to be a black shirt in the prison during your stay in Srebrenica, your imprisonment in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I received that shirt in the hotel in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were -- what clothing were you wearing while you were imprisoned in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no clothes. I only had my shorts. I was stripped of everything else. I had this blanket given me by the turnkey Cude, and I covered myself with that blanket while I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, to your knowledge, the things that Veselin Sarac and Mr. Nevenko and yourself have spoken about in this interview, are they true?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what Sarac said, two things are not accurate. I am trying to be as accurate and honest as I can. First of all, there was no power at the time, no electricity, so when they said they used electricity to hurt him on his sex, I don't think that's true. And the second thing, when he said that sometimes there were ten or 12 people beating us, that's not true because that number of people could not fit into that room. Whenever they beat us, there were no more than two to four. And what Nevenko said and what I said is true. I agree with his statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there comes one time in the video when you were speaking and you say that you were in combat when you were captured. Did you consider yourself to be in combat when you were captured?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe that because when I was with this piece of mining equipment, there was shooting from Bijelo Polje. At the village of Kutuzari, they were shooting at this mining machine. The driver was in the cab, and two operators were down there in the fork. I was holding this M-48 rifle that I didn't have issued to me personally because we carried only two rifles whenever we went to get water. I had only six Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. rounds therefore, and I didn't shoot them in the direction of Bijelo Polje, not all. I later gave that rifle to Krnjo and set off towards Bracan, not knowing that Bracan had been captured by Muslim -- what shall I call them? It was not the army, not the civilians, but a mixture of both. Let's call them Muslim forces. So I believe that since I was shooting at them and they were shooting at me, it was combat. Of course, I ran out of ammunition, then I dropped my gun. I no longer had a weapon or ammunition at the moment when I was captured. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to turn to a final set of questions and I will be finishing soon, Your Honours. Can you just give me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. I do have to ask the registrar for a new number for what is P98.1E, and that's a revised transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think we'll do it the same way we did yesterday. We'll put dot 1.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The previously appended transcript had the number P98E. And the new -- the transcript tendered today gets exhibit number P98.1E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, both of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just assume that that would be moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, I just want to return quickly to one or two points, and you testified previously that on the 25th of September your teeth were pulled out by pliers by a person called Kemo. Afterwards, you testified that your mouth was disinfected by urine. Now, did someone urinate into your mouth after your teeth had been pulled out?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That person was Kemo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so when you said that your mouth was "disinfected by urine," were you saying that a bit ironically and facetiously?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were you being ironic; in other words, cynical, about it? Ironic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you consider the fact that Kemo urinated into your mouth a medical practice that was actually going to help your mouth after that point?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That answered the question, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, you have referred to someone who supposedly is Naser Oric at several points in your testimony. The person who you said that you saw on three occasions while in prison that referred to himself as Naser Oric, did you ever see that person or an image of that person after you left the Srebrenica prison?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I watched a videotape, I believe it was, and if I had known I would be coming here I would have probably brought it. On that videotape I saw Mr. Naser Oric on horseback.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what colour horse he was on? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think white.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any other occasions to see the person referred to Naser Oric or an image of the person referred to as Naser Oric, whether as a photograph, in print, or on a tape, or television after that point?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Afterwards, when Mr. Oric had come to The Hague and when he was saying to this Honourable Court that he was not guilty, this hearing was broadcast where I live.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the person that you saw on that broadcast the same person that you saw on three occasions in the prison in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Sellers. Mr. Jones, you have two -- the option of starting now or have the break now and start immediately after. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I think the break now would be preferred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have -- you'll not finish today for sure?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So just to put you in the picture, Mr. Jones, and also the Prosecution, I have been advised by the -- or we have been advised by the Victims and Witnesses Section not to take this sitting until the end, to proceed, say, for about another hour or so. Reason is that we have a little bit of a problem. The witness is feeling a little bit tired and congested, and we will proceed for another hour or until -- or even earlier if he's not in a position to continue testifying today. That obviously -- this doesn't in any way affect your -- the time you need -- require to finish your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite all right, Your Honour. And we understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Radic, now we are going to switch sides, we are going to the Defence, and Mr. Jones, who is co-counsel for Mr. Oric, will be putting a few questions to you. Not a few, actually quite a few. Cross-examined by Mr. Jones:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Radic -- you can see I'm over here. You told us yesterday how Mr. Kukic was killed by Kemo on the second night that you were in the SUP, which would be the 25th of September 1992, and you were an eyewitness to that.

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I'm going to start by asking you some questions about that incident. Now, when Kemo started to hit Kukic, Kukic cursed Kemo's and Mrki's Ustasha mothers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we're all familiar, probably, with this curse in your language. Is what Kukic said: "Fuck your Ustasha mothers"?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for the benefit of everyone, "Ustasha" was a famously brutal puppet government of the Nazis in Croatia during the Second World War. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to answer this question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, surely you've heard of the term "Ustasha" before. What does that mean to you?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ugly, an ugly term. To me it's a slur when you hear somebody called Chetnik or Ustasha; it's the same to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Ustasha government was responsible for the deaths of tens of thousands of Serbs and Jews, wasn't it, during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to say "Fuck your Ustasha mother" is a terrible insult, isn't it? It's like in the West saying: "Fuck your Nazi mother"?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it about the most insulting thing you can say to someone in your language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it depends who this someone is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps. Let me move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't it on hearing that curse against his mother that Kemo flew into a rage and hit Kukic on the chest with a log?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's most likely that he was irritated by that curse, and then he hit him with that split log on the chest, as he would have done with me, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was more than irritated, wasn't he? Isn't it a fact that he flew into a terrible rage when he heard that insult and he was out of control at that point?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it's no reason to kill a man because of one word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course not, Mr. Radic. I wouldn't suggest that for a second. What I'm seeking to establish with your testimony is that it was that provocation, whether justified or not, which led to Mr. Kemo to lose his self control. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case I can accept that. I too would be angered by something like that, but I certainly wouldn't kill a man over it. I could perhaps hit someone, maybe even more than once, but I would never do something of the kind Kemo did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Absolutely. But isn't it right that it was that single blow, or it was a single blow by an enraged Kemo that killed Kukic, after hearing this insult?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a single blow with that split log.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Kemo then immediately tried to revive Kukic with water, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was too late at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The witness said "da," it wasn't interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't hear him say "da." Did you say "da," Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get the impression from all of this that Kemo didn't mean to kill Kukic?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't answer that. Probably not. If he had known this blow would kill him, he probably wouldn't -- although I'm not sure. I don't know, really. I don't think -- I can't believe he was inhuman enough to kill a man. Only Kemo knows for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next day, the next morning, Kemo asked you if Kukic was alive, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- no, no. He asked us what had happened to him, if he was alive or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he found out -- when Kemo found out that Kukic was dead, didn't he immediately take steps to conceal the fact that Kukic had been killed by disposing of the body that morning?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kemo knew that very evening, that very moment, that Kukic was dead. He didn't need to wait until the morning. He knew right away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But the next morning he immediately disposed of the body in some unknown location.

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when Kemo asked you what happened to Kukic the next morning, did you understand that as a sort of hint that you were to keep silent as to how Kukic really died?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak about myself. I don't know about the others. That would certainly have. I understood that. But I can't tell you about the other detainees, what their opinion was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But for yourself, then, you understood that as a message to you that you should keep silent that Kemo killed Kukic?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you replied to Kemo that Kukic died of a heart attack or a stroke, indicating indeed that you were going to keep secret that fact. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't me who answered. It was one of us, the prisoners, who said that he had suffered a heart attack, not a stroke in fact, a heart attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you first saw the person who you said introduced himself as Naser, which I think was a few days later, you said that no one was beating you and that Kukic died of a heart attack.

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Naser asked us if anyone had beaten us, and we said not. In relation to Kukic we said that he had died as a result of a heart attack. Personally, I feared for my own fate. I feared that I might suffer the same fate as Kukic, and for that very reason, I did not dare say that anyone had beaten us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact you did keep it secret from everyone else in the prison, including this person calling himself Naser, that Kemo had killed Kukic. You kept it a secret.

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I should rephrase that. Did you keep it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you are on the same wavelength.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you think I'm referring to your co-detainees. You kept it secret from the other Muslims in the prison that Kemo had killed Kukic. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The prisoners who were with me saw that he was dead when he was brought back to the cell. Of course they realised he had been killed. As for the other Muslims, I didn't tell any of them or meet any of them, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the person who called himself Naser asked about Kukic and you said that he died from a heart attack, didn't he say, "Why didn't you tell me? We could have got a doctor."

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could refer you to your 2000 statement in May 2000 to investigators of the ICTY, which was referred to yesterday -- and we have copies for everyone if need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have it, too, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the witness should be given a copy of it so he can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In the English version it's page 9 of 12. ERN 02030472, and it's the first two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, in your version it's page 8, paragraphs 8 and 9. Do you see that page 8, paragraphs 8 to 9 on your version. Naser Oric asked: "What happened to Kukic? "We said he had a heart attack during the night." Naser Oric asked: "Why didn't you report his illness? We would have brought him a doctor." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. You remained silent. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, I really don't remember saying that. If I did remember, I would certainly say so. It's possible, it's just that I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can keep the statement with you. I'll be referring to it again subsequently. In terms of beatings you also told us yesterday that Kemo and the others hit you on the chest mostly in order to avoid leaving visible marks. You said, and I'll refer to the transcript, it's page 57, lines 3 to 6: "There were no visible injuries. They would beat us from the waist up, on the chest, on the back, that sort of thing. They hardly ever hit us or punched us on the face in order hard to cause an injury that would have been visible."

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did state that and that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Isn't it right then that the people who beat you didn't want there to be signs that they were beating you?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And weren't you told to clean up when important people came to the prison; told to wash your face and to clean your wounds?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have enough water to drink let alone wash. There was a shortage of water in Srebrenica at the time. The reservoir had been mined or it had been shut down, I'm not sure which. So they, too, used the springs nearby for their own needs. We couldn't have any drinking water except when Cude was around. And I remember that twice a police officer in uniform came to bring us water, but not the rest of them. We would not have any water for half a day at a time, not even to drink let alone to wash our faces. There was a shortage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did on one or two occasions, did you not, wash your faces to clear the signs of wounds, injuries, at least before you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the 16th of October, 1992, the morning that we set out to be exchanged. That was the first time I washed my face while --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not true to say that when important people came to the prison you were told to wash your faces? That's not something which is correct?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know if I stated that. I don't remember. If I did, I really don't remember. My apologies. Maybe it was misinterpreted or mistranslated, but I certainly don't remember ever stating anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can come back to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Jones. Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: May I have a question to the Defence. The statement you are referring to, was it made by Mr. Radic? If I am right in my memory, a statement which you presented to him was made by one of the witnesses whom we saw in the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: It was not -- I don't remember that Mr. Radic made this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's something I wanted to check, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- I don't even think, I'm positive that Judge Eser is correct, or is right. It was someone else, not the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Nonetheless, the answer is helpful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So since the guards, Kemo and others, were trying not to leave visible signs of injury, isn't it right that there weren't actually many visible signs on your face that you had been beaten when you were in the prison?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was a wound inside my mouth when my teeth were extracted, but that was inside my mouth therefore it could not be noticed. My jaw is still a bit disjointed because all of my teeth had been injured. Therefore, I did have a number of internal injuries, but you couldn't see them on the outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in fact it wasn't obvious to someone who saw you in the prison that you had been beaten, just on your physical appearance?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in terms of physical appearance, on my chin you could see specks of curdled blood. I didn't shave for a while, therefore my beard had grown, therefore there were some marks that you could notice, and my physical disability at the time, too, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to that, the injury you referred to on your chin. We saw you on the video a moment ago, and in fact there aren't visible marks of injury on your face in that video, is there? I won't replay it.

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when the footage was made. Most probably, based on what I have been told -- I didn't know at the time that there was a camera at the hotel in Bratunac during our exchange. I only found out when I came here to testify before the Tribunal. As for the marks on my chin, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. when I arrived in Bratunac they had a lavatory there; we washed-up, and of course I removed those marks from my chin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't you also wash up before your exchange, that was when you were still in Muslim territory?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you couldn't wash the whole thing away. The water was cold and the marks were solid, were curdled, and there wasn't enough water to go around. We all of us only had a single bottle of water to wash up, and it was just not enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, dealing with the others for a moment, Nevenko, Zoran, and Sarac, isn't it correct that most of the injuries we could see on the video were caused either when they were beaten on the day of the exchange by Kemo, which you've described to us they were taken off the truck and beaten, in other words after they left the prison, and then also in Potocari when some other people came and beat you? In other words, aren't the injuries that we saw on them injuries which were caused after they left the prison for the most part?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarac did have some visible injuries before that, and Nevenko because Nevenko was not beaten on the day of the exchange, only Sarac and Zoran. At Potocari, no one beat us. I deny that. I'm not sure who stated that in the first place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sarac was beaten on the day of the exchange after he left the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he was returned to the building from the lorry, to the SUP building, and that's when he was beaten, both Sarac and Zoran. And then they were again returned to the lorry. The postman and myself, we hoisted them up onto the lorry. And at Potocari, no one beat us or mistreated us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these beatings on the day of the exchange occurred after the last time that you saw the person who called himself Naser, because you saw him on the 15th of October, the night before?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that was the next day, the 16th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the beatings on the 16th of Sarac and Zoran were pretty severe, weren't they, from what you could tell?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Weren't those beatings in fact worse than any beatings they'd received prior, when they were detained in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. They made them walk and then we had to hoist them up onto the lorry. And once they'd been exchanged, we sat them down. During the transport, we used the same tractor to go back that had brought the bodies, the bodies to be exchanged. And then they returned to Bratunac. They were lying on the tractor. They were suffering too much pain to even sit up. It wasn't me, after all, who was suffering their pains, therefore I can't describe that for you. They would be best placed to speak about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I said I'd return briefly to the subject of the injury on your chin. You'd been beaten before you ever came to the SUP, weren't you, on the day of your arrest?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had injuries from those beatings.

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the beatings you sustained when you were arrested, when you were walking along, as you described, with the other two prisoners, being kicked and beaten, and then when you were on the truck going to Srebrenica again being beaten, you say that left no visible marks on your body whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact is you were beaten before you came to the SUP.

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you saw this person who called himself Naser, you didn't say to him this injury on my chin, if he could see it, this happened while I was in prison, as opposed to happening beforehand? It's not something you said to him?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you accept, do you, that the person, this person, may not have known that you had been beaten in the prison at all on the basis of what he saw?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that calls for speculation. I just want to raise the objection for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, objection sustained. Please rephrase your -- you can easy to rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll return to that when I come to the theme through another route.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that a lot of the time that you were in the prison that the cell was very dark. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. At night, obviously, there was no electricity. And Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. even by day, there was a small opening in the wall, some sort of a window, 60 by 50 centimetres was the size, and that was the only opening for the light to come into the cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was September, October, so coming on for winter. Is it right that the days were very short, so it was dark both in the mornings, early mornings, and early evening?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in fact it was very hard to see any real detail of people's faces in the cell?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was difficult to see, that's one thing; secondly, there were no visible injuries on our faces, and please allow me to set you right on this. The last time you said -- I did not have any injuries on my chin. There was blood from my mouth from when my teeth had been extracted. So that's where the blood came from, from inside the mouth. I didn't have any external injuries on my chin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was congealed blood, it had dried?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the day, was there more light in the hallway outside your cell than there was in the cell itself, if you follow what I mean? Was the light coming in from the hallway?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you couldn't have light coming in from the hallway because the main hallway ran the whole length of the building. And the only light it received was from the entrance door. There was a small corridor between the entrance door and our cell. The corridor itself was even darker than our cell, therefore no light could have come from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in fact when you looked out from your cell, you were looking into even greater darkness?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because there was another door outside the cell and then the corridor, that when you opened that door you would be out in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us there was a window in the cell but it had no glass. According to the --

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- standards at that time, that was quite normal, wasn't it, because most of the buildings in Srebrenica didn't have glass because of aerial bombardments and shellings. Is that something you're aware of or able to help us with?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I had no opportunity to walk around Srebrenica and to see for myself. I was brought to the SUP building on the evening of the 24th, and I never left the building except when we picked Kukic up outside the building. I wasn't able to see whether it had any windows or not. I wasn't even trying, there was no time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you heard, when you were detained, the sound of incoming fire; shells, mortars, bombs, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear that. Maybe twice throughout the time I spent there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said it was too small to lie down in your cell, but I think it's right to say that when we saw the video yesterday there appeared to be a mattress there. I'm not suggesting that that was there at the time. But isn't it right that you could actually lie down full-length, there was enough space for a man to lie down in your cell?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can only have one person lying down on the mattress but not five or six persons, and that's how many we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally on the subject of the cell: The bars which we saw also looked too small for someone to be punched through the bars. Is that right? Did anyone ever punch you or the others through the bars?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There was enough room between the bars. For a person to put their fist through, you had to come close. They would grab you by the hair through the bars, and then they would hit you against the bars. Of course it was possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you some questions about visits by the person who you said introduced himself as Naser Oric. Now, first -- first, no one else introduced themselves in that way, did they? They didn't say, "I am Kemal Ahmetovic," or "I am Mrki," or anything like that? No one introduced themselves to you, did they?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion Akif came over. I do remember that, but I wasn't asked about that, not now and not when I gave my statement. That was before he was killed, he came to see us, he was standing in front of the bars. He said his name was Akif. He was wearing military uniform, combat uniform. And he said that there would be an exchange and that we were to be treated in compliance with the Geneva Conventions. That was the first and last time I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This man was in his 40s or something, was he?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say exactly. He was rather short and wore a moustache. I do remember that, but I can't give you his age. It's very difficult for me to say. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it somebody who appeared to be too old to be, as you say, the person Naser's nephew?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How should I know? I don't know whether it was a nephew or not. It's just something I heard. Again, I say I'm not positive but I heard that he was the uncle of Mr. Naser, but I can't be certain about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll come back to that. Presumably the first time that Mr. Naser came and introduced himself, that was the first and last time. In other words, there wasn't a need for him to introduce himself every time he came to your cell.

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't know Naser Oric before the war, did you?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just to be clear, you never -- at the time, anyway, you didn't identify Naser Oric in the sense of seeing someone you knew as Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. When you saw this person who called himself Naser, you didn't identify him as someone you knew. You based yourself on who he said he was.

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know him. He just introduced himself as Naser, and I accepted it for what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, today you told us that subsequently you saw a video in which the person was on a white horse. Now, you don't know that that person was Naser Oric, or do you?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do because this is a tape that I watched after my exchange. This may have been in 1990 -- I can't be certain about this, but I think 1993 or possibly 1994. It was a year or two after my exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that video, didn't the person you're calling or you're identifying as Naser Oric have a beard? The man on the white horse, doesn't he have a beard?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't the person who you said called himself Naser clean-shaven?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was clean-shaven with a crewcut, short hair, when he came to see us. But I think if I see a person on three different occasions, for me that was evidence enough for me to recognise the person even 20 years later, let alone a year or two later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take that one step at a time. Mr. Radic, a beard is an important feature, isn't it, of someone's physical appearance, important feature in identifying them?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I, too, sported a beard when I was exchanged, but now I don't. I don't think you would recognise me based on that, though, with or without the beard. I could grow a beard now, but for me that would be no answer still. I am positive 100 per cent that the man on horseback was the same man who came to our cell and whom I saw on three different occasions while detained in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because I am not -- There are two things. Between his previous answer and your last question, he answered something else which failed to show in the transcript, that's number one. Number two is on page 38, line 3, it says: "I don't think you would recognise me based on that, though, with or without the beard." I think it should be I don't think -- I don't think you wouldn't recognise me, or rather, he's saying that I think you would still recognise me, but not as it is in the transcript. In other words, are you saying that if we -- one looked at you when you had grown a beard and one looked at you when you were clean-shaven, one wouldn't be able to recognise you just the same or that you are still recognisable, with or without a beard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe the mistake is mine, but with or without the beard, with or without hair, if I know a person, I know them and I can recognise them with or without a beard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us you saw this person who called himself Naser three times. These were all brief occasions, weren't they, just a few moments.

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were in the darkness that you've described, the darkness of your cell, apart from the third occasion which we'll come to. Isn't that right, the first two occasions was in the darkness of the cell you've just described to us?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not such darkness that you couldn't see a man. It was light enough to see a person. Otherwise Naser came to the cell by day and we could see him in daylight and we could remember his face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What time of the day would that be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in the morning, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was it three times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twice. The next time we saw him was in a different room, on the 25th, on the eve of the exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. Sorry, Mr. Jones, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So twice in the morning, which you agreed was dark in the mornings. You also agreed earlier that it wasn't possible to see details, real details on people's faces. On the video the person you're identifying as Oric has a beard; in the cells you're saying he was clean-shaven. What was the distinctive feature which you picked up on? Was it the blue eyes which you've identified Mr. Oric as having, or was it some other feature? What was it that was the distinctive feature that you came to recognise?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His face itself. That was quite enough. I know, recognise, Mr. Naser even now. It's the first time I actually saw him here, but it's like we were there together yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at the description which you gave of the person who you saw and who you say was Oric in your interview in 2000 to ICTY investigators. It's in your version page 7, the first paragraph. In our version it's page 7 of 12, ERN 02030470, the third paragraph. Do you see that, Mr. Radic? Page 7, first paragraph. I'll read it for you.

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't even look at this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's page 7, first paragraph in your version: "I will describe him for you. Naser Oric had a strong build. He was not tall, maybe 160 centimetres. He had dark brown hair and was clean-shaven. I think Naser had blue eyes. He was quite young. I don't think he was even 30 years old at the time," which was 1992. "He was dressed in a yellow khaki beige-green camouflage uniform, which is called an American uniform. On the left breast pocket of his shirt he wore a patch that had lilies on it. It was a special uniform." Do you recall giving that description?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about the second occasion when you say that you recognise Naser Oric which is when you saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment now because Judge Eser would have a question at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I have a question with regard to the darkness in the morning. Mr. Radic, the Defence counsel stated so twice in the morning, which you agreed, was dark in the morning. You also agreed earlier that it wasn't possible to see details. Now, was it dark the whole morning? The morning lasts, for me, from -- until 11.00 or 12.00. Was it dark the whole morning or was it only dark in the early morning and it became lighter later on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. You couldn't see details, that's what I meant. What I meant actually was that you couldn't discern the details of injuries on our faces, but you could see a person. It was light enough. It was day, after all, not nighttime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Eser. Mr. Jones, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to round up on that subject. Is it right then that there isn't any single specific physical feature which you can point to which you recognise -- which you say you recognised later when you saw Naser Oric and recognised him? You just insist that you recognise him. Would that be a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. 12 years is a long time; a person can change considerably even in a few months, physically I mean. One can put on a lot of weight or lose a lot of weight, get sick, get ill. There could be all sorts of circumstances. But when he came to our cell and later when I saw the videotape, I claim with 100 per cent certainty that it was the same person, Mr. Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Radic, and sorry to insist on this, but it is: There is no feature, is there, which you're pointing to? It's not his eyes, it's not his nose, it's not his hair, it's not his beard because that's changed, it's not his height or his clothes. There's no feature which you're telling us you recognise, not a single feature.

utterances.speaker: Nedjelko RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, that's what you meant. Of course there are such features. His face mainly, his hair changed a bit. He was -- he had a short haircut at the time. But his face didn't change. It was a lot thinner then, but his appearance, the picture of it, the picture of his face I have in my mind is the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned his hair -- I'm sorry, but face is still unspecific.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It looks like the witness is in discomfort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Exactly. What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just two things. I would like to please say that right now counsel is insisting, I believe, that he has the answers that he wants. And second, if the witness needs to take a break, we should stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Either take a break or stop, as we had agreed to do, because I can notice that the witness is a little bit distressed at the present moment. Mr. Radic, let's go to private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure you understand, Mr. Jones. I mean, I wouldn't have opted for this particular moment, but at the same time you have cleared up the main questions that you needed to put to the witness on this particular point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, there's absolutely no problem at all with us in interrupting. We're sensitive to witness concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I may, obviously, need to resume on this subject. I haven't finished it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, this is precisely what I meant to say. I know that you haven't finished, and I wouldn't have preferred to interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- when we haven't actually closed this chapter. However, things being what they are, I see no particular prejudice. We can stop now and give Mr. Radic a rest. He is not feeling well, and I'm sure that these two days -- two and a half days that you have now you can relax a little bit, nurse the throat infection that you have, make sure that they give you the treatment that you need for it so that on Monday you'll be able to return to this courtroom fresh and in the position to continue and finish the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Usher, please could you escort the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's it. I think we need to adjourn at this point in time. We will continue with this witness on Monday. I think we also ought to be planning to have the next witness available on Monday, because I would imagine that you won't require the entire sitting, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, I -- no, I didn't get that far, obviously, so I would need at least another two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you don't need the entire sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I would suggest that you will have the next witness in line available at some point in time on Monday between the first and the second break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We will do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure you will, Mr. Wubben. So I think we need to -- yes, I think we need to stop here. I mean, we have no other business to transact at this point. We will resume on Monday at 9.00 in the morning in Courtroom I. And I wish to thank the Victims and Witnesses Unit representative, who is not here in the courtroom at the moment, who has helped monitor the situation for us in order to make sure that the witness does not suffer any distress. I can assure you that that unit does their work and its work in a very professional way. I thank you all and I wish you a nice weekend. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 17th day of January, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.44 a.m.,
